> The art is amazing, and the game itself is significantly different from 
> MtG.  Anybody else with first impressions?

Um, I don't like it.  I bought a starter deck and four boosters.
After going through the cards, I only found four pieces of art
that I actually like (Zip Gun, Cryptic Mission, Cloak the Gathering,
and Zebulon).  All the others are just too dark and morbid.

I've shown the cards to two other big fans of MtG and neither
one could actually finish looking through the cards I showed them.
They just handed them back and said, "No more."

At the local game shop, the attitude was subdued.  Several boxes
of Jyhad were sitting untouched on the counter.  A couple of the
regulars had bought a few packs and were struggling to comprehend
the rules.  Most of the heavy investors in MtG hadn't bought any
Jyhad and weren't planning to.

I'm sort of regretting that I spent $20 on the game.  When is
INWO going to be released?

-- Bill

first saw the Gathering.  Part of it is that I'm not really into the whole

In article <reecewCusu1A.7A4@netcom.com> reecew@netcom.com (Reece T. Watkins) writes:
>I don't even think it should be billed as 
>a Deckmaster game, since te only thing it has in common with MTG is 
>Tapping cards.

Actually, there is more than just tapping in common between the two
games. Here are some of the similiarities:

* Sacrificing "life" points to perform some action
* "Unique" cards
* Playing "effects"
* Blocking actions

The games really are quite similiar, particularly if you compare a
creature oriented game of MtG with Jyhad. In that case, the "essence"
of each game is the same:

1. "Summon" creatures.
2. Attack opponent with creatures.
3. Opponent can attempt to block creatures.
4. If a creature is blocked, then combat ensues.
5. Switch sides and repeat until one side is dead.

--
Michael Wang

Messages.Author: Randall P.
Messages.Body:
To the nay-sayers, let me point out that Jyhad does a remarkable job of 
duplicating the gothic-horror feel of its source material, the 
role-playing game Vampire: the Masquerade. The World of Darkness 
portrayed there is a grim, dark, hostile place where vampires are both 
the hunters and the hunted.
  In general, I found the level of artwork more consistent in Jyhad than 
in MtG. It is not geared to making the power decks of Mtg, either. The 
emphasis is very much on the strategies of dealing with the cards that 
come into play. The political intrigue can play a major part in bringing 
down your prey.
  As far as being true Deckmaster or not, it most certainly IS true 
Deckmaster. It was never supposed to be the Second Coming of Magic, but 
to be a trading card game designed by Richard Garfield. I think THAT is 
what makes it true Deckmaster, rather than how closely it approximates 
Magic gameplay.

  As to the future expansions, it would be easy enough to incorporate new 
Disciplines specific to the non-Camarilla clans. I am waiting for the 
Sabbat to make their dread appearance. can anyone say 300+ card 
expansion? Werewolf, Mage, Wraith, and Fairie would all make excellent 
sources, and could actually give the game depth far beyond Magic.

  Give it a chance, folks...

  Randy

Surprisingly, I was in the other big hobby shop today and they
also had plenty of Jyhad Boosters sitting on the counter (and
they sell everything at 10% off, so the boosters were only 
$2.50).  As I remember, Legends and The Dark didn't spend more
than 2 or 3 hours on store shelves.  And here, Jyhad has been
out for three days and only 10% of the preordered cards are 
available, and Boosters are still widely available.

So, it looks like WotC made another brilliant move.  They only
printed 10% of the preorders to test the market.  From what I
can see of the local gaming market, Jyhad will only be slightly 
more popular than that "S" card game. Soon, WotC 
will come to the conclusion that 180 million cards is about
twice what their retailers could ever sell.  Even though they
could force the retailers to honor their preorders (forcing many
of them to take big losses), they will take pity on them and
make an announcement they they will reduce the print run and
only print about 80 million cards instead of 180 million.  That
will allow them to get The Dark out sooner and maybe get Fallen 
Empires out on time.  IMHO.

-- Bill

Time for a reality check (no flame bait intended).  Jyhad came out
earlier than many people expected.  A lot of people are still
checking it out and learning about the game.  In _some_ areas
it may seem to be off to a slow start, but also realize many places
are having no problems selling Jyhad cards.

A few pointers:  It was never thought that Jyhad would overtake MtG
in popularity or replace it as a game of choice.  MtG is quicker
and easier to play (before rules lawyering).  From the first previews
of Jyhad, most of those who had played it were billing it as a Gamers'
Game.  So all the kids who are buying Barney Pogs and Magic Cards
aren't buying Jyhad.  So what?  So all the business types that play
MtG during lunch breaks aren't buying Jyhad.  So what?  These people
have a perfectly enjoyable game already to play.  That does not mean
Jyhad is going to flop.  Just because Risk has sold less copies than
Monopoly does not mean Risk is a failure of a game.  I know many
people up and down the entire length of California who are putting
MtG on the back burner so they can play Jyhad.  At least two friends
of mine who played MtG from the very start are working on selling
of their entire collections so that they can focus on Jyhad.  It's
just more of their style of play, just as I prefer to play Risk
over Monopoly.

And one last thing.  When the TSR flop came out, it was appearent
pretty quickly that it was a flop.  Both here on the net and out
in the Real World, a majority of opinions on the game seemed to be
negative.  I'm not going to say Spellfire was a bad game (never
played it), but I'll point out that the same backlash does not exist
now.  Look at how many articles in this news group have Jyhad in
the subject and consider how small a percentage negative comments
seem to be.  Anyways, post what you think about the game, and please
say why.  If you have a reason for disliking the game, hopefully
someone who thinks as you can avoid the mistake of investing in
Jyhad.  I just am trying to avoid out of hand dismissals that the
game is going to die because nothing can compete with the One True
Game.


Anyways, this stretched out far longer than I intended.
Cheers,
Chris.
cat@wintermute.ucr.edu

> out for three days and only 10% of the preordered cards are 
> available, and Boosters are still widely available.

I got into Magic while Antiquities were out. The first couple of months that
I was playing the game, I could buy as many Unlimited and Antiquities as I
wanted, since everybody had them. About the time Revised came out, the
environment changed, perhaps in part because people suddenly realized that
not *all* of these cards would always be available (Black Lotus, etc.)
Suddenly people were more interested in "getting them while they were hot." 
Legends and the Dark sold out in a feeding frenzy, and Fallen Empires should
certainly be preordered to guarantee availability.

Thing is, Magic has been around a year or so now, and it's gotten very hot.
Because Magic is hot, we apparently believe the Jyhad should be every bit
as hot. I don't doubt that Magic cards (like the Unlimiteds and Antiquities
I saw when I started) languished on many dealer'shelves until the game
built up momentum. Why should we expect anything different from Jyhad?
It hasn't even been out a week, and already some are predicting its demise
because there are still cards on the shelves.

Digo, pacience y barajar (What I say is, patience, and shuffle the cards).

Messages.Author: J Greely
Messages.Body:
In article <6ZSRBUQS@math.fu-berlin.de> bing@its.bldrdoc.gov writes:
>WotC is planning on printing 180 million Jyhad.  That tells
>me that they intend for Jyhad to be nearly as popular as MtG.
>I don't think that will happen.

It is not clear how much of that initial limited print run is based on
distributor and retailer pre-orders, so I would hesitate before making
assumptions about WotC's intentions based on the print run.  It may
simply be that the retailers and distributors don't want to lose out
on the chance that it *might* be as hot as Magic.

  Is it?  Well, it's gone from the two stores I frequent most, and
they had a fair amount.  They're getting more, and I'll buy more, and
apparently a lot of other people are at least getting their feet wet.
I suspect most of the speculators will hang back on buying cases, in
case it turns out to be just a success.

>Yes.  I watched a couple of months ago as a couple of kids sold
>off their entire Magic collection and bought hundreds of packs
>of that "S" card game.

Spellfire was an obvious hack, quickly thrown together in an attempt
to cash in.  While WotC has obviously rushed Jyhad a bit to make it by
GenCon, their rush job is thought out a lot better than Spellfire.
They've done a good job of taking the basic Deckmaster frame and
producing a very different game out of it, with a lot of promise.  I
don't agree that it's cooler than Magic, mostly because I haven't had
a chance to play a complete game yet, but I'm interested enough to
give it a chance.  As a game, though, not a lifestyle; I *might* buy
one box of boosters if I sell my old car off, but not otherwise.  I'm
done with pouring money into a bloody card game.

>Yup.  There is a certain percentage of MtG players that will get
>into Jyhad and never look back.  But, I think that most will play
>it for a bit, and go right back to MtG.

You leave out the folks who will play both indefinitely, as well as
the card collectors who'll buy most anything with pretty pictures on
it.  Jyhad will never be the game we play over lunch at work, but it
has the potential to be something we frequently play in the evenings.
Ask me again in a few weeks.
--
J Greely (jgreely@synopsys.com)

Messages.Author: Tom Wylie
Messages.Body:
<bing@its.bldrdoc.gov> wrote:
>> A few pointers:  It was never thought that Jyhad would overtake MtG
>> in popularity or replace it as a game of choice.
>I wonder about that.  From recent posts on this board, I hear
>that there are 220 million Magic cards in circulation and that
>WotC is planning on printing 180 million Jyhad.  That tells
>me that they intend for Jyhad to be nearly as popular as MtG.
>I don't think that will happen.

The print run for Jyhad and for Magic: the Gathering is determined entirely
by preorders.  Distributors preordered 180 million Jyhad cards, so at
least that many will be printed.  Boom, there ya go.  The 220 million
Magic cards figure is only accurate up through the end of June...  The Dark
Alone added, what, 80 million to that?

We don't "intend" for Jyhad to be more or less popular than Magic, but I
think most people anticipate that it won't sell as well in the long run.
That is fine.  As long as more people are having fun because Jyhad exists
than would be if it didn't, then the game will have accomplished its
mission...  equalling the sales of Magic is not and never will be the goal
of any Deckmaster game.  We wouldn't complain if Jyhad did sell as well ;)
but we aren't making policies based on trying to make it do so.

>I'd agree with that.  And serious games historically do not
>sell as well as "goofy" games.  My point was that WotC had
>better be careful, since Jyhad won't sell nearly as well as MtG.

Who says it has to sell as well?  We certainly don't.  It would suck if it
failed to the point where some store goes out of business because it can't
pay for the Jyhad cards it ordered, but I don't think that's going to happen.

>> I know many
>> people up and down the entire length of California who are putting
>> MtG on the back burner so they can play Jyhad.  At least two friends
>> of mine who played MtG from the very start are working on selling
>> of their entire collections so that they can focus on Jyhad.
>Yes.  I watched a couple of months ago as a couple of kids sold
>off their entire Magic collection and bought hundreds of packs
>of that "S" card game.  It was all the rage for a couple of weeks.
>I don't see those kids much anymore.

On the other hand, how many people in the groups you play in play both
Magic and Spellfire?  Not saying that you *should* play both, but if
they were the only ones playing Spellfire and not Magic, then it doesn't
particularly surprise me that they wouldn't migrate to where the Magic
groups meet.  I.e., are they not playing at all, or are they just
playing somewhere else?


Tom Wylie		rec.games.deckmaster Network Representative for
aahz@hal.com			Wizards of the Coast, Inc.

Messages.Author: Gary Smith
Messages.Body:
bing@its.bldrdoc.gov wrote:
: Surprisingly, I was in the other big hobby shop today and they
: also had plenty of Jyhad Boosters sitting on the counter (and
: they sell everything at 10% off, so the boosters were only 
: $2.50).  As I remember, Legends and The Dark didn't spend more
: than 2 or 3 hours on store shelves.  And here, Jyhad has been
: out for three days and only 10% of the preordered cards are 
: available, and Boosters are still widely available.

How many of you purchased MtG when it first came out? I remember
seeing this game sitting in the stores for quite awhile before
I picked it up. I don't normally go in for the vampire genre,
but I decided to try something I don't normally (and under peer
pressure :] ) and I think this is an excellent game so far. The
rule booklet is a bit unwieldy, but we were able to play reasonably
well the night we purchased the game. Now, we switch back and
forth between MtG and Jyhad because they are fairly different
from one another and they offer respite from each other.

@@ <-- 2 cents

--Gary (mage@jimmy.harvard.edu)

Messages.Author: tahelia c powe
Messages.Body:
Nearly everyone I know, if not everyone, has dropped Mtg for the time 
being to investigate Jyhad.  My favorite comic books/gaming store sold 
out in both locations within two days, and they were limiting pack 
purchases.  However, strangely enough, other stores still have them.  I 
think that has to do with the fact that those of us who frequent my 
favorite store didn't realize Jyhad was still available elsewhere.  All 
the starter decks are gone, but some boosters are still around.  We get 
together quite a bit to play; most of us have gone so far as to buy 
the Vampire counters, although the blood bags aren't popular because    
it's hard to get the counters back in.  

  As for what happened with the `S' game, when I first walked into the 
store to buy some, my friends said `It sucks.'  The guy who owns the 
store said a few people had bought them.  At present, he is still 
trying to figure out a way to get rid of it.  Based on my observations, 
I'd have to say there is no logic in comparing reactions to `S' and 
Jyhad.  When I called about Jyhad, the attitude was uncertain, but, as 
you can see, they were certain about that other company's game.  (In 
case it's not clear, I called the store owner to see how my friends 
like Jyhad when it came out, rather than running down like I did when 
Spellfire did). 

  People are already putting together sets.  In short, I feel quite 
confident in saying that the gobs of people with whom I play LOVE 
Jyhad, even though we admit it's a longer game.  As for lunchtime, I 
don't play Jyhad then, as I did with Magic, but I certainly take that 
time to attempt to make my Jyhad deck more competitive  :). 

  Hmm, I forgot to mention one thing.  One store I called about Jyhad 
didn't even seem to know that they were getting any before the official 
release date, so I suspect they told a lot of interested players that 
it would be a few weeks.  Perhaps that could explain why they still 
have boosters.  

Tahelia C. Powe
Magic/Jyhad addict 
tcpowe00@mik.uky.edu
